title: Traffic pattern synthesis and stress validation notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects an experiment-first playbook for synthesizing production-like traffic mixes and running stress/throughput validation against the serving runtime. Focus is on deterministic repeatability, controlled chaos injection, and validating graceful degradation when we saturate components (GPU queue, request-coordinator, cache).

High-level goals:
- Produce a small suite of canonical traffic recipes (steady, mixed-burst, diurnal spike, microburst + background) that map to real-prod trace percentiles.
- Ensure runs are repeatable across runs and machines (seed/entropy hygiene).
- Validate end-to-end saturation: identify which layer (network, coordinator, kernel, memory) first breaks and instrument obvious signals.
- Produce a short checklist so oncall/bench team can run the stress tests with minimal setup.

Key constraints and guiding principles:
- Keep latency SLO obligations in mind: we care about sustained throughput at P95 latency constraints, but stress tests intentionally ignore cost to find failure surfaces.
- Reproduceability over synthetic realism when triaging: have both calibrated realistic mix and a minimal deterministic stress mode.
- Avoid heavy priming state that obscures root cause (i.e., run both cold and primed variants).

Traffic recipes (canonical):
1) Steady-concurrent (baseline):
   - Poisson arrivals with lambda tuned to target concurrency C under typical seq len distribution.
   - Seed RNG with fixed value.
   - Duration: 20m (5m warmup + 15m steady).

2) Microburst-with-background:
   - Background: low-rate Poisson at 10% of capacity.
   - Microbursts: short rectangular bursts that push to 200% of target throughput for 10-30s, repeating every 2m.
   - Jitter: add +/- 15% random jitter on burst start times.

3) Diurnal-swing (for long runs):
   - Sinusoidal modulated arrival rate over 6h to test autoscale and cache eviction dynamics.

4) Primed-cold comparison:
   - Prime run: run 10k short prompts to warm KV caches then steady run.
   - Cold run: clear caches, restart runtime, then run same steady recipe.

Hybrid randomness/seed policy:
- Use two-layer seeding: (1) global RNG seed for arrival times/traffic shape; (2) per-client seed for prompt selection. Record both seeds in run metadata file.
- For determinism in loadgen we pin distributions (no system time-based entropy beyond controlled jitter).

Warmup strategy (why and how):
- Warmup exists to stabilize runtime kernel selection, warm CUDA kernels/JIT, and to populate path-dependent caches (KV, tokenizer model caches).
- Recommended default: 5m warmup for typical runs, but include a 15m warmup variant for long-run stability validation.
- Warmup should use representative prompt mix, not just microbench single-token prompts.

Instrumentation and signals to capture:
- Request-level: client-side start/first-byte/last-byte latencies, token throughput, error codes.
- Runtime-level: request queue lengths per worker, GPU utilization (SM/mem), PCIe bandwidth, GPU memory occupancy, HV cache hit/miss rates, kernel dispatch latency histogram.
- Orchestration-level: number of inflight coroutines, backpressure events, worker restarts/OOMs.
- System-level: NIC drops, TCP retransmits, disk IO if model sharded.
- Export all metrics to bench-run namespace in observability so we can correlate.

Failure mode fingerprints (quick heuristics):
- Queue buildup + steady GPU utilization low -> coordinator/serialization bottleneck.
- GPU saturated (SM% high) + rising P95 -> compute-bound.
- GPU utilization low + high PCIe traffic -> memory transfer bottleneck / KV cache churn.
- Large variance in first-byte latencies across workers -> cache priming imbalance or uneven tokenization costs.

Example loadgen config (YAML-ish snippet to paste into bench-tools config):
---
name: microburst-with-background
seed: 20251104-01
duration: 00:20:00
warmup: 00:05:00
clients: 64
arrival_pattern:
  background: {type: poisson, rate_per_client: 0.25}
  burst: {type: rectangle, amplitude: 2.0, width_s: 15, period_s: 120, jitter: 0.15}
prompts: {corpus: ./corpora/mix-small.json, distribution: categorical}
measurements: [client_latencies, rpc_errors, server_queue_length, gpu_metrics, kv_cache_hits]
---
(bench-tools will translate into concurrent clients with per-client arrival scheduling. Keep the seed constant for repeat runs.)

Run checklist (quick):
- [ ] Confirm bench machine time sync (ntpd).
- [ ] Upload seed/metadata file to s3://bench-runs/<run-id>/meta.json.
- [ ] Clear or record KV cache state depending on cold/primed variant.
- [ ] Start observability collectors with correct tags.
- [ ] Run with --record-trace on first attempt for 2m to capture perf counters.

Acceptance criteria (for a throughput regression run):
- Baseline steady run achieves >= 95% of historical median throughput at target P95 latency.
- Microburst recovery time < 30s to return within 110% of baseline latency envelope.
- Cold vs primed delta documented and < X% (TBD per model; add thresholds per-model in model-catalog).

Post-run forensics template (copy into run notes):
- Run id: 
- Seeds: global / per-client
- Config file path: 
- Raw artifacts: bench logs, server traces, GPU traces, observability link
- Short summary: what failed / what held / suspected layer
- Next action (e.g., file perf PR, throttle, hardware repro)

Open questions / next experiments:
- How much does tokenizer variability (multi-language prompts) affect priming stability? Quick test: run identical seed with language-balanced corpora and compare kernel selection variance.
- Should we add a "half-primed" mode that primes only KV but not kernels (fast path to isolate kernel vs cache issues)?
- Can we fold a lightweight chaos injector to flip network latency on a subset of workers to simulate cross-AZ noise?

Notes to self / todo:
- Add a small python script to compute expected concurrency given arrival lambda, average processing time, and tokenization variance. That will help auto-configure client counts.
- Produce a short runbook for SRE with the above checklist + link to the most recent regression dashboard.
- Iterate on acceptance thresholds per-model and publish under product-qa.

References and related runs:
- RWF-2143: "bench-tools: deterministic arrival scheduler" (Linear ticket)
- PR #86 bench-tools: adding burst scheduler (github)
